title: Priesthood and temple blessings: lives, restrictions, and the 1978 revelation
introduction: This history follows Black Latter-day Saints whose faith and service continued while priesthood and temple restrictions limited their participation. Their lives help us understand both what was withheld and what changed in 1978.

sections.title: Elijah Able: ordained, serving, and still asking
paragraphs: Elijah Able, whose name also appears as Abel, joined the Church in 1832. In Kirtland in 1836, Ambrose Palmer ordained him to the Melchizedek Priesthood. He participated in washing and anointing in the Kirtland Temple, and Zebedee Coltrin ordained him a Seventy. His service took him to New York and Canada as a missionary. Later he worked as a carpenter, raised a family with Mary Ann Adams, and helped build the Salt Lake Temple.

His life also exposes the distinction between holding priesthood and receiving later temple ordinances. Although he retained his priesthood standing after the racial restriction was announced, his request to receive his endowment and be sealed to Mary Ann was denied. Another request was refused in 1879. The earlier Kirtland ceremonies did not mean that he had received the later endowment. He continued in the Church until his death in 1884. His service and his exclusion belong in the same account.

sections.title: The restriction and the people it excluded
paragraphs: In 1852, Brigham Young publicly announced that men of Black African descent could no longer be ordained. Black people could still join the Church through baptism and confirmation. Over the following decades, restrictions also excluded Black women and men from temple endowment and sealing. These were profound limits on participation, including the opportunity to covenant in the temple and be sealed as families. They did not amount to a prohibition on every ordinance: some Black Saints performed baptisms for deceased relatives.

The Church’s current historical explanation states that no revelation establishing the restriction is documented. The record should therefore not be filled with a supposed divine reason. The racial ideas used to defend the restriction have been rejected by the Church. Knowing when leaders publicly announced a policy is different from knowing a revealed explanation for its origin.

sections.title: Jane Manning James: faith with an unanswered petition
paragraphs: Jane’s own remembered life reaches beyond the petitions preserved in institutional records. In the autobiography she dictated near the end of her life, she wanted her faith and experience to be heard at her funeral. Her life included family responsibilities, help given to neighbors, and devotion sustained through hardship. She remembered her belief in Jesus Christ’s gospel as stronger in old age than when she first joined the Church.

Between 1884 and 1904, Jane repeatedly approached Church leaders about receiving her endowment and being sealed. In 1888 she received permission to perform baptisms for deceased relatives. In 1894, leaders arranged a unique proxy sealing that placed her in Joseph Smith’s household as a servant. That arrangement did not grant the endowment and family sealings she had sought. Jane died in 1908 without receiving them during her lifetime. Her endowment and family sealings were performed on her behalf in 1979. Remembering her faithfully requires hearing both her testimony and her persistent request for blessings withheld from her.

sections.title: Faith that crossed borders
paragraphs: By the 1970s, the question touched believers across several continents. Black and mixed-ancestry members in Brazil contributed toward the São Paulo Temple while knowing that the restriction would keep some of them from its ordinances. In Ghana and Nigeria, groups studied the restored gospel and asked the Church to send missionaries. These were people seeking baptism, service, and a place in a worshipping community—not merely an administrative question about ancestry.

Revelations in Context describes a letter from Emmanuel Bondah, a schoolboy in Ghana, asking Spencer W. Kimball for a Book of Mormon and help in becoming a Church member. Kimball was moved to tears. By early 1978, he was repeatedly praying in the temple and inviting his counselors and the Apostles to study and pray about extending ordination and temple blessings. The lives of those waiting were part of the history of that seeking.

sections.title: June 1978: prayer, confirmation, and an open way
paragraphs: On June 1, 1978, President Kimball met with members of the First Presidency and Quorum of the Twelve in the Salt Lake Temple. Gordon B. Hinckley, who was present, later recalled discussion followed by a prayer voiced by Kimball. His account describes a shared assurance through the Holy Ghost that the time had come to extend priesthood blessings without the racial restriction. This is the experience the participants testified of: a sacred spiritual confirmation received as they prayed together.

The First Presidency’s announcement was dated June 8 and released to the news media on June 9. It opened ordination to worthy men without regard to race or color and temple blessings to worthy members and their families. On September 30, N. Eldon Tanner presented the revelation in general conference, where those assembled sustained it unanimously. Official Declaration 2 preserves the announcement and its acceptance; it is not a transcript of the private prayer.

sections.title: Receiving the blessings and rejecting racism
paragraphs: The change reached women as well as men through access to temple ordinances and family sealing. It did not create priesthood ordination for women. For families who had waited, the opened way meant concrete opportunities to serve, make covenants, and receive ordinances together. Jane’s ordinances in 1979 also connect the new access with the life of someone who had asked long before the revelation.

Today the Church rejects teachings that connect Black skin with divine disfavor or supposed failure before birth, oppose marriage across races, or rank one race above another. Its current teaching calls members to repent of prejudice and help remove racism. These commitments belong beside the history, not outside it. Learning these lives can move us toward more careful listening, truthful remembrance, and a willingness to welcome one another in the community of Jesus Christ.
